en: The preceptor who has taken the vows, who has recited the mantra, who is greatly compassionate, who possesses realized knowledge through recitation, who is skilled in the performance of protective rites and offerings, and who is capable of extracting the thorns [of affliction] and the like. [2.1]
One who has exerted great effort in the knowledge of mantras should examine a site that is free from thorns and other such defects, ensuring it is level and not merely small or inferior. [2.2]
Whether on a mountain or in a forest, in a monastery or a garden,
on the banks of rivers or in the wilderness— wherever the mind finds delight;
provided it is free from gravel, stones, husks, charcoal, clods of earth, and rocks.
For the acquisition of land must be performed with intense purity; therefore,
one should exert effort regarding food and [the construction of] monasteries, groves, cities, villages, ports, and so forth.
Observe from the east onwards, up to the north itself:
ground that is low or high must be abandoned; ground sloping toward the northeast should be accepted.
If it is elevated in the center, there will be sovereignty or even the status of a Vidyādhara.
If the ground is elevated toward the north, there will be death or the loss of wealth;
if the ground is elevated toward the east, the destruction of the family will swiftly occur.
When the ground is depressed in the center, the practitioner perishes there.
Then, the ground endowed with the [auspicious] characteristics is inspected by the preceptor. However,
while the mandala is being drawn, if it is in the eastern direction, there will be the death of the king and the occurrence of various calamities for the people.
And in the southern direction, whoever the mandala is intended for, that very person dies there; such is the teaching of the best among those who know the scriptures. [2.10] (Note:
Who is this authority? Is it Jñānapāda?)
If the teacher is in the western quarter and the entry is from the north,
or if it occurs in the region of the south-eastern direction, there will be a great downpour of rain.
One should predict the danger of famine if it occurs in the corner between the southern and western directions.
If it is being drawn in the northwestern direction, however, wind and rain will arise.
If near a funeral pyre, there will be death; if over a place presided over by a nāga, there will be water.
If in the shade of a tree, one would take away a child; therefore, a location other than those is best.
There too, the ground should be known as fourfold, according to its color and so forth, in sequence:
the four types are Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, and Śūdrī.
The Brāhmaṇī ground is to be known as white, while the Kṣatriyā is considered yellow.

The Vaiśya woman should be known as red, while the Śūdra woman is proclaimed to be black. On a white patch of ground, one should prepare a cane seat, a water-pot, a staff, a rosary, or a sacred knowledge.
On a site that is of superior measure, level, smooth, free from saline soil, devoid of defects, sloping toward the northeast, and delightful, one should further purify it. [2.17]
One should discard within a distance of one cubit from the hand any skull, hair, roots, bones, chaff, stones, gravel, ash, charcoal, insects, or living creatures.
If there is stone, a great wind arises; if there is bone, the occurrence of piercing pain results.
If it contains gravel, there will be muteness; if it contains husks or charcoal, there will be fever.
If it contains hair, roots, wood, and the like, minor calamities will arise.
Therefore, one who desires auspicious results should carefully purify the plot of ground.
In mountain caves or groves, or on the shores of the great ocean;
or in a primordial *siddha*-site, or especially in a cremation ground or an open space. (2.21) [If there is no other available space?]
In these places and divisions, no purification need be performed;
rather, one should purify the site equally according to one's ability, as well as the maṇḍala. [2.22]

The Vajrācārya himself should perform the mandala practice there; the wise one may even fashion the mandala with ashes at the appropriate time. According to his capacity, according to his enthusiasm, and according to the wealth that is available—
The great yogin should act in such a way, or else perform a mental construction. For who is capable of accurately conceptualizing the mandalas?
Through union with one's own presiding deity, the construction of the maṇḍala is accomplished.
It should be drawn with divine powder or with medium-quality powder;
or with powders made of the five precious gems, or with rice and so forth. Having thus constructed the maṇḍala according to one's means, [2.26]
One should sprinkle the wealthy disciple, but the indigent one facing the cloth [paṭa].
Alternatively, for one who is virtuous, [one may use] gold dust or the like.
A wise person who desires supreme accomplishment should construct it to a hundred cubits in size.
It should be blue with sapphires, great sapphires, and royal silk; and red with rubies, great rubies, and excellent coral. [2.28–29]
Then, from the red [pigments] of Vajratuṇḍa and Mahātuṇḍa, Śyāmaka is produced;
that which has the color of Puṣparāga and Nuvara is proclaimed as Pīta (Yellow). [2.30] % [Regarding the word *anne*, it is likely *abhyāṃ*?]
White is considered to be made from pure crystal powder or conch;
blue, red, deep black, yellow, and likewise pale white—these are the desired colors for kings, since a king indeed possesses great wealth. [2.31]

Now, there may be a householder who is wealthy, an ornament of the earth. [2.32] % NB In these cases, where the initiates are wealthy—including the king—the cloth painting (paṭa) is entirely out of the question; see 34.

For that [mandala], one should indeed fashion a mandala measuring one hundred cubits with colors possessing the previously mentioned characteristics and mixed with fragrant saffron, according to the prescribed rules. Furthermore,
a wise person should not construct that mandala on a cloth.
Or a merchant, or a caravan leader, who is faithful and endowed with wealth,
should prepare it with delightful and great stages interspersed with jewels.
Or else, one may fashion it with pigments such as glass, vermilion, and orpiment;
or with powders made of the five precious gems, or with rice flour and so forth.
Having understood this according to what is appropriate, the wise person should cause the mandala to be made.
The handspan for kings is one hundred; for vassals, half of that;
for guild-masters, half of that is prescribed; and for caravan leaders, twelve. [2.37]

Half of that is for those who are foremost among practitioners; this sequence of the mandala has been taught. Furthermore, according to the scriptures, one should draw it oneself with proper reasoning and according to one's capacity. [2.38]
The ritual procedure for the *argha* offering is taught first; second is the acquisition of the ground (*bhūparigraha*);
third is the *tippasūtra*; and the fourth is the *jñānasūtra*. [2.39]
What is the *Anne-ṭippisūtra*?

The fifth is the falling of the dust, the sixth is the consecration of the jars (*kalaśādhivāsana*), the seventh is the placement of the jars (*kalaśanyāsa*), and the eighth is the accomplishment of the mandala (*maṇḍalasādhana*). [2.40]
The ninth is the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and the tenth is considered the rite of oblation (homakriyā);
the eleventh is the dismissal (visṛṣṭi)—thus it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
[2.41] % NB Q/R Tattvasaṃgraha

Now, first of all, the sequence for the fire-oblation (homa) and the arising of its trees and so forth: one should abandon the *aśvattha* tree in the eastern portion and the *arjuna* tree in the south-eastern (āgneyī) direction. [2.42]
The *aśvattha* [tree]— [this is the emendation; the manuscript reads *aśvatthe*]—
and the *plakṣa* on the southern side,
while the *palāśa* is for the *jātudhānaka* (or *jātudhānajā*, according to the variant).

One should avoid the *nyagrodha* tree in the west, and one should abandon the *śālmalī* in the northwest. One should avoid the *bakula* tree in the north, and also the *udumbara* in the northeast. || [2.43] || Here, one should also know the "site-nāga" (*vāstunāga*) which lies according to the sequence of the directions.
During the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, the serpent faces west;
its head is on the left side, and it has the form of a man facing south.
Likewise, during the three months beginning with Phālguna, it faces the direction of Kubera (the north).
Furthermore, the sequence for the sides is declared according to the western head;
during the three months beginning with Jyeṣṭha, one should sleep with the head toward the north.
Then, during the three months beginning with Bhādrapada, the Vāstu-nāga faces the east.
In the months beginning with Bhādrapada, as the sun proceeds through its transits facing south,
he sleeps everywhere at the end of the site-sections on his left side.
Having ascertained the place of the serpent’s bed, the wise man should dig in the lap-section;
he should dig the earth to the depth of a knee if he desires the highest accomplishment.
The father, the son, and likewise the wife perish at the head;

on the back, however, there would be the destruction of oneself, and then exile from one’s country occurs. At the tail, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth will surely perish; such is the sequence of the hoods. || 2.49–2.50 ||

One should know that the seven constellations beginning with Kṛttikā are in the east, those beginning with Maghā are in the south, the constellations beginning with Anurādhā are in the western part, and those beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā are in the northern direction. [2.51]
On a day purified by the moon and stars, the wise one should perform [the rite].
On that beautiful site of earth, preceded by the community of monks,
and accompanied by other recipients of offerings as well as artisans and laborers.
Seated upon a comfortable throne, adorned with all ornaments—
or else wearing a golden ring on his right hand—
endowed with the three concentrations, preceded by offerings and music.
One should draw the maṇḍala on ground smeared with an area the size of a cow’s hide.
Therein, the one rich in wisdom should worship the Earth-deity in the center;
having looked toward the hosts of gods in the east, he should worship the Guardian of the Field in the south.

Having likewise worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings the Buddhas together with their sons— the *anne-pālakas* in the west and the *yakṣas* in the north— one belongs to the Nāga family.

The wise one should offer milk-rice and the like to the Earth, and to the Deity, rice with curd, as well as dried meat and onions. To Kṣetrapāla and Kuvera, he should offer [food] filled with liquor and blood.
Having recited the mantra over the vessel of food offerings, one should lie down upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
One should personally perform the binding of protection for all the disciples with the mantra:
*oṃ mohani svāhā*.
The knower of yoga should perform the washing of the face with this mantra:
*oṃ dattili svāhā*.
Having offered one thousand and eight white mustard seeds mixed with sandalwood to the obstructors, [he should proceed].
Having recited the mantra for the directions, the practitioner should cast it away and sleep in the posture of the bed of Nirvāṇa. [2.61] Now follows the sequence for requesting the earth.
At dawn, one should offer the bali; if it is auspicious, one should predict prosperity. But if the omen is indeed inauspicious, the wise person should perform a rite of pacification (śānti).
Then, the glorious one, accompanied by a bell and holding a vajra and a ritual scoop (kaṭacchuka), [should proceed].
He should say: "Today this untroubled land has been acquired by me; therefore, with devotion, that which is to be done must be performed by you as my assistants. [2.63]
Having recited this with diligence and having performed the scattering of flowers,
one should summon the assembly of disciples and consecrate the water-offering (argha) and the ritual jars—
ten, five, or even one— provided they are free from the "black thread" defect.
[They have] bodies marked with well-cooked signs, with long necks and hanging lips; their necks are adorned with shimmering yellow garments, and they are radiant, smeared with chalk. [2.66]
[He asked: "O Mother, what is the *kaṭhinī*?
[She replied: "It is filled with excellent water containing the five trees, medicinal herbs, and jewels;
it is covered everywhere with mango sprouts and its neck is draped with flowers. [2.67]
In this manner, one should indicate the insignia upon those jars thus characterized:
the insignia of the Krodhas on ten sides, and the insignia of the Jinas on five.
But on a single insignia of the Enemy of Obstacles (Vighnāri) in the filaments of the universal lotus,
one should place either the moon or the sun in their respective locations according to the application of their own mantras. [2.69]
It is called the universal lotus.
"The universal lotus indeed has petals red like the dawn in the directions starting from the east; its petals in the directions of wind and fire possess a yellow hue;
and those in the directions of the Lord of Pretas and Īśāna are dark green like *dūrvā* grass and black like a blue lotus. Thus [it is said].
—Q Nāgabodhi?
Now, the symbols of the wrathful deities are indeed described here according to the scriptures:
the symbol of Yamāntaka is a vajra-mallet (*vajramudgara*). [2.71] (Is it a vajra or a mallet?)
[One should visualize] the white staff of Prajñāntaka, the lotus of Padmāntaka,
the crossed-vajra of Vighnāri, and the dark-green sword of Acala. [2.72]
But the mudrā is also [the same] as that of the utterance of "hūṃ."

Furthermore, that mudrā of Ṭakkirāja is described by the adept as follows: "Having wrapped the ring fingers and extended the middle fingers, one should place the tips of the wrathful ring fingers pressed against the thumb. [2.73] Thus it is said.
The name of Nīladaṇḍa is likewise "the great power," and his weapon is the club;
the mudrā of Uṣṇīṣa, however, is the black añjali.
Or one should fashion the black, formidable vajra of Sumbharāja;
one should draw all the emblems situated upon a sun disk on a double lotus within the ritual jars.
Then, having wound them with threads spun by virgins or with silk cloths, [one should proceed].
Having established those water-pots in the northeast corner,
one should scatter white mustard seeds in the ten directions for the sake of protection,
together with grains of rice.
And by uniting with the three samādhis, drawing up the water of the celestial river (Svarṇadī),
one should cause it to enter the interior of the jar through the application of mudrās and mantras:
OṂ TAPTE MAHĀTAPTE HŪṂ SVĀHĀ.
Having recited this seven times, one should bring water from the Gaṅgā; then,
having placed it along with flowers and a *mālāvajra* upon the vase,
one should wrap leaves around the left hand with those very same flowers.
Holding the rosary with the right hand, one should recite the *hūṃ* syllable eight hundred times,
or half of that, or two hundred times.
Then, with *bhaktajaḍī*, followed by *siddhārtha* and *nimba*,
having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should cast them into the fire and then into water.
Taking up the incense burner, one who recites the verses of the five families should recite:
"Akṣobhyavajra, great wisdom, Vajradhātu, great sage!"
O you who are the three mandalas, the foremost of the three vajras, O Vajra of Sound, homage be to you! Vairocana, the greatly pure, the vajra of peace, the great delight!
O supreme among the supreme, naturally luminous, Vajra of the directions, homage be to you!
[2.83] O King of Jewels, profound as the ocean, Vajra of space, stainless as the sky, pure by nature, untainted, Vajra of Body, homage be to you! [2.84]
O Vajrāmṛta, Great King, free from conceptual construction, holder of the space-vajra; O Vajrāmita who has attained the perfection of passion, Vajra of Speech, homage be to you! [2.85]
O perfectly awakened Amoghavajra, fulfiller of all hopes,
arisen from the nature of purity, Vajrasattva, homage be to you!
[2.86] Having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel nut as well,
Having offered even camphor, and having indeed sounded the bell, one should dismiss [the deity]. (2.87) [ghaṇṭāṃ nadan] is conjectured; the manuscript reads *ghaṇṭānādaṃ*.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the consecration of the water jar (kalaśa).
